subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Lower extremity nerves: hip and thigh
vignette: A 54-year-old man has burning neuropathic pain radiating from an inguinal hernia repair incision toward the suprapubic region. Sensation is diminished just above the pubis, and motor strength in the legs is normal.
question: The sensory loss is best localized to which region?
explanation_correct: The iliohypogastric nerve (T12-L1) provides sensory innervation to the suprapubic region and is commonly injured during inguinal hernia repair, producing burning pain radiating to the inguinal and suprapubic area. It also supplies motor fibers to transversus abdominis and internal oblique. The distribution matches this patient's suprapubic sensory loss.

explanation_incorrect.A: The scrotum and labia majora are supplied by the genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2).
explanation_incorrect.B: The anterolateral thigh is the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2-L3) distribution.
explanation_incorrect.C: The medial thigh is supplied by the obturator nerve (L2-L4).
explanation_incorrect.D: The anterior thigh and medial leg are the femoral nerve (L2-L4) distribution.

educationalObjective: Localize iliohypogastric sensory loss to the suprapubic region after inguinal surgery.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Lower extremity nerves: hip and thigh
vignette: A 30-year-old man undergoes laparoscopic pelvic surgery and later notices reduced sensation over the upper medial thigh and anterior thigh beneath the inguinal ligament, along with an absent cremasteric reflex on the affected side.
question: Which nerve is most likely injured?
explanation_correct: The genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2) supplies sensation to the scrotum/labia majora and medial thigh and motor fibers to the cremaster. Injury during laparoscopic surgery decreases upper medial and anterior thigh sensation beneath the inguinal ligament and abolishes the cremasteric reflex. The absent cremasteric reflex is the key localizing sign.

explanation_incorrect.A: Iliohypogastric injury causes suprapubic and inguinal pain, not an absent cremasteric reflex.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lateral femoral cutaneous injury causes meralgia paresthetica with anterolateral thigh burning and no motor or reflex deficit.
explanation_incorrect.D: Obturator injury causes medial thigh sensory loss and weak adduction and does not affect the cremasteric reflex.
explanation_incorrect.E: Femoral nerve injury weakens knee extension and reduces the patellar reflex.

educationalObjective: Recognize genitofemoral injury by loss of the cremasteric reflex after laparoscopic surgery.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Lower extremity nerves: hip and thigh
vignette: A 38-year-old woman in her second trimester reports tingling, numbness, and burning pain over the anterolateral aspect of her thigh. There is no weakness, and symptoms are attributed to compression under the inguinal ligament.
question: Which nerve is compressed?
explanation_correct: Compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2-L3) causes meralgia paresthetica: tingling, numbness, and burning pain in the anterolateral thigh. Risk factors include tight clothing, obesity, pregnancy, and pelvic procedures. It is a pure sensory nerve, so there is no motor weakness.

explanation_incorrect.A: Femoral nerve lesions cause anterior thigh and medial leg sensory loss with quadriceps weakness and a decreased patellar reflex.
explanation_incorrect.B: Obturator lesions cause medial thigh sensory loss and impaired adduction.
explanation_incorrect.C: Genitofemoral lesions affect the scrotum/labia and medial thigh and the cremasteric reflex.
explanation_incorrect.E: Iliohypogastric lesions cause suprapubic sensory changes after inguinal surgery.

educationalObjective: Identify meralgia paresthetica as lateral femoral cutaneous nerve compression.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Lower extremity nerves: hip and thigh
vignette: A 62-year-old woman has reduced sensation over the medial thigh and difficulty adducting the thigh after a pelvic operation.
question: Which nerve is most likely injured?
explanation_correct: The obturator nerve (L2-L4) supplies sensory innervation to the medial thigh and motor fibers to the obturator externus, adductor longus, adductor brevis, gracilis, pectineus, and adductor magnus. Injury during pelvic surgery decreases medial thigh sensation and weakens adduction. It is the classic nerve injured in pelvic operations.

explanation_incorrect.B: Femoral nerve injury weakens leg extension and the patellar reflex with anterior thigh sensory loss.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lateral femoral cutaneous injury is purely sensory and causes anterolateral burning (meralgia paresthetica).
explanation_incorrect.D: Genitofemoral injury affects the cremasteric reflex and scrotal/medial thigh sensation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Iliohypogastric injury produces suprapubic and inguinal incisional pain.

educationalObjective: Link pelvic surgery with obturator nerve injury and weak thigh adduction.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Lower extremity nerves: hip and thigh
vignette: A 45-year-old man sustains a pelvic fracture with a retroperitoneal hematoma. He cannot extend his knee, has a decreased patellar reflex, and has reduced sensation over the anterior thigh and medial leg.
question: Which nerve is injured?
explanation_correct: The femoral nerve (L2-L4) supplies the quadriceps, iliacus, pectineus, and sartorius and provides sensation to the anterior thigh and medial leg. Pelvic fracture, retroperitoneal hematoma, or psoas abscess can compress it, producing decreased leg extension and a decreased patellar reflex. Loss of the patellar reflex localizes the lesion to the femoral nerve.

explanation_incorrect.A: Obturator injury causes medial thigh sensory loss and weak adduction, with intact knee extension and reflexes.
explanation_incorrect.B: Sciatic injury affects posterior thigh and below-knee sensation with weak knee flexion, not the patellar reflex.
explanation_incorrect.D: Lateral femoral cutaneous injury is sensory only and cannot weaken knee extension.
explanation_incorrect.E: Genitofemoral injury affects the cremasteric reflex and medial thigh/scrotal sensation.

educationalObjective: Recognize femoral neuropathy from retroperitoneal hematoma by loss of knee extension and the patellar reflex.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Lower extremity nerves: hip and thigh
vignette: A 27-year-old man sustains a posterior hip dislocation in a motor vehicle collision. He has weakness of knee flexion and loss of sensation over the posterior thigh and nearly all of the leg below the knee, with sparing of a narrow medial strip.
question: Which nerve is injured?
explanation_correct: The sciatic nerve (L4-S3) supplies the posterior thigh, posterior knee, and all below-knee sensation except a narrow medial band. It innervates the hamstrings and adductor magnus and splits into the common peroneal and tibial nerves. Posterior hip dislocation, herniated disc, and piriformis syndrome are classic causes. The spared medial strip reflects preserved femoral (saphenous) supply.

explanation_incorrect.A: Femoral nerve lesions affect anterior thigh/medial leg sensation and knee extension, not posterior thigh and below-knee sensation.
explanation_incorrect.C: Obturator lesions affect medial thigh sensation and adduction.
explanation_incorrect.D: Superior gluteal lesions cause Trendelenburg gait from gluteus medius/minimus weakness.
explanation_incorrect.E: Inferior gluteal lesions weaken gluteus maximus, causing difficulty rising and climbing stairs.

educationalObjective: Localize posterior hip dislocation deficits to the sciatic nerve with sparing of the medial leg.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Lower extremity nerves: hip and thigh
vignette: A 50-year-old man develops burning pain radiating from an inguinal incision to the suprapubic region after hernia repair. The injured iliohypogastric nerve (T12-L1) also carries motor fibers to which muscle?
question: Which muscle receives motor innervation from this nerve?
explanation_correct: The iliohypogastric nerve (T12-L1) supplies motor fibers to transversus abdominis and internal oblique in addition to suprapubic sensory innervation. It is commonly injured during inguinal hernia repair, causing neuropathic pain radiating to the inguinal and suprapubic region. Internal oblique is therefore the correct motor target.

explanation_incorrect.A: The cremaster is supplied by the genitofemoral nerve, not the iliohypogastric.
explanation_incorrect.B: Quadriceps femoris is innervated by the femoral nerve.
explanation_incorrect.C: Adductor longus is innervated by the obturator nerve.
explanation_incorrect.E: Gluteus maximus is innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve.

educationalObjective: Recall that the iliohypogastric nerve motorically supplies transversus abdominis and internal oblique.
